background.definition: Pancreatic cancer is a ductal adenocarcinoma of the exocrine pancreas.

list.listitem: Pancreatic cancer is the fourth most common cause of cancer-related death among US men.
The incidence is roughly equal between the two sexes. African Americans have a higher incidence than white Americans.
Review of the US CDC's SEER database demonstrates that even allowing for sociodemographic factors, survival is worse for African-Americans than for white Americans.
Risk factors for pancreatic cancer include cigarette smoking and obesity.

The risk of pancreatic cancer is 9 times higher in patients with Lynch syndrome. The absolute cumulative risk of developing pancreatic cancer among patients with the syndrome is 1.3% at 50 years and 3.7% at 70 years.
Risk is increased following thymectomy.

A genetic predisposition may be present in up to 5% of patients. A mutation of the p16 germline has been reported in families with pancreatic cancer and melanoma. An excess of pancreatic cancer is also seen in families harboring breast cancer susceptibility gene-2 mutations.
There are no effective screening tests for pancreatic carcinoma at the present time. C
USPSTF recommendations of 2019 propose that no screening should be undertaken in asymptomatic adults without specific high risk (Peutz-Jeghers or inherited familial risk). B.

A 2020 consensus guideline on screening high risk populations outlines those who may be at increased risk and recommends early investigation if they develop diabetes, but the guideline acknowledges lack of evidence base. C

A prospective cohort study identified 165 persons with a mutation putting them at 10% or greater lifetime risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and 201 relatives of mutation carriers who were mutation negative. They performed endoscopic ultrasounnd (EUS) and MRI with MR cholangiopancreatography annually for a mean of just over 5 years. During that time 9.3% of mutation positive and 0% of mutation negative participants were diagnosed with PDAC. However, average survival was only 18 months, with a range of 1 to 32 months, and only 3 of the 10 were diagnosed at an early stage; 4 had metastases at the time of diagnosis.
Suspect pancreatic cancer in middle-aged or older patients with weight loss or jaundice. C
Initial imaging is with ultrasound or helical CT using pancreatic protocol. B
The diagnosis can be confirmed by endosonographic FNAB. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Abdominal pain improves after a meal
Pain is associated with diarrhea and fatty stools
Pain has a burning quality and radiates substernally

list.listitem: Suspect pancreatic cancer in any middle to older age patient with chronic deep upper abdominal pain and/or nausea. Weight loss (≥15 pounds) and obstructive jaundice are often present.
The sudden onset of type 2 diabetes in patients 50 years or older may also indicate a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.
Courvoisier's sign (a distended and palpable gallbladder in the presence of jaundice) is often present in these patients.

A case-control study of 120 consecutive patients with pancreatic cancer and 180 age and sex matched controls found that the following signs and symptoms were more common in patients with pancreatic cancer: appetite loss (OR = 41), pale stools (OR = 31), abdominal pain (OR = 30), jaundice (OR = 20), unusual bloating (OR = 20), unusual belching (OR = 17), weight loss (OR = 12), and dark urine (OR = 10).
Tests such as AST, Lactate dehydrogenase, serum albumin, amylase, carcinoembryonic antigen, and alkaline phosphatase are of very limited value in diagnosing pancreatic cancer.

When pancreatic adenocarcinoma is suspected, options for imaging include ultrasound and spiral abdominal CT scan. A dynamic-phase helical or spiral abdominal CT performed according to a defined pancreas protocol is preferred by the ACR appropriateness criteria (rating = 9) but ultrasound is a good alternative (rating = 8). Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is more accurate than abdominal ultrasound.
Echo-enhanced power doppler sonography is usually not available, but if it is, it is highly sensitive and specific.

Final diagnosis may be made with endosonographic FNAB, which is the most sensitive and specific test. FNAB is not always necessary, as most pancreatic surgeons will consider operating on a patient if the abdominal CT is highly suggestive of pancreatic cancer.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is a useful diagnostic tool in patients for whom the CT scan is equivocal since fewer than 3% of patients with pancreas cancer have normal pancreatograms.

PET with 2-[18]fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose, while not used routinely in the diagnosis of pancreas cancer, may help differentiate between chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer, thus avoiding surgery in some patients.

In patients in whom abdominal CT has detected resectable pancreatic cancer, preoperative CA 19-9 may detect which patients have truly resectable disease. Patients with a CA19-9 levels over 256.4 U/mL are likely to have unresectable lesions at surgery (92% sensitive, 82% specific, LR+ 5.1, LR− 0.1).
ACG guidelines note that most pancreatic cysts are asymptomatic and have a low likelihood of malignant transformation.

Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) can be low-risk or high risk, the latter characterized by the presence of mural nodule or dilated pancreatic duct. The 5 year risk of malignancy or high grade dysplasia is 3.1% in low risk IPMNs and 9.8% in high risk IPMNs.
For patients who are not surgical candidates, no further evaluation is recommended.

Patients with a cyst that has low malignant potential (serous cystadenoma) or a pseudocyst do not require further evaluation. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is the recommended test for patients where diagnosis is likely to change management, i.e. cyst with high risk appearance and symptomatic patients.
For patients with jaundice or an associated mass, referral for EUS with fine needle aspiration is recommended.
For patients with a history of pancreatitis, pseudocysts should be followed clinically. If the cyst may be causing acute pancreatitis, referral for EUS-FNA is recommended.

For patients with a cyst that is not clearly non-neoplastic, do not have a history of pancreatitis, and do not have jaundice or associated solid mass, AGA guidelines (2018) recommend the following. If the main duct is >5 mm, cyst ≥3 cm, or there is a change in the main duct diameter with upstream atrophy, referral for EUS-FNA should be considered. If none of those conditions are met, surveillance MRI annually for 1-2 cm lesions and every 2 years for <1 cm lesions is recommended. For lesions 2 to 3 cm in diameter that appear to be an IPMN or mucinous cystic neoplasm, a shorter surveillance interval or EUS in 6 to 12 months is recommended.
In assessing the pathology of pancreatic cancer, it appears that increased PD-L1 expression is associated with worse survival and higher nodal status.
The Harvard Cancer Risk Index can be used to predict an individual's risk of pancreatic cancer.
A clinical decision rule has been developed to estimate prognosis for patients with spinal metastases from a variety of primary tumors, including pancreatic cancer.
Recently developed risk scores can help predict morbidity at surgery and readmission risk following surgery.
Consider pancreatic cancer in middle-age or older patients who present with deep upper abdominal pain, weight loss (>15 pounds), or obstructive jaundice.
Initial imaging is with ultrasound or dynamic phase helical or spiral CT performed according to a defined pancreas protocol.
The diagnosis may be confirmed with endosonographic FNAB preferably with a 19-gauge needle. This technique may be used no matter where the lesion is in the pancreas.
Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) is still the treatment of choice for carcinoma of the head of the pancreas without evidence of extension or metastases. B
If the patient is in poor medical condition or if the tumor is determined to be inoperable on initial evaluation, obstructive jaundice may be palliated by endoscopically placed metal stents. B
Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel prolongs survival in patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, can provide clinical benefits, and can improve quality of life. B

Gemcitabine prolongs survival in people with advanced or metastatic pancreatic cancer and can give clinical benefits and improve quality of life. A large RCT compared gemcitabine alone with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, and found that median survival was better with the combination (8.5 mos vs 6.7 mos, p <0.001). One year survival was increased (9% vs 4%, NNT = 25).
There may be some benefit from gemcitabine/capecitabine combination compared to gemcitabine alone in advanced disease.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend chemotherapy plus radiation as superior to chemotherapy alone in patients with advanced pancreatic cancer.

Most experts recommend initial neoadjuvant chemoradiation as opposed to initial surgery in patients staged as having borderline resectable disease. This is supported by a recent meta-analysis demonstrating improved overall survival with neo-adjuvant therapy compared to upfront surgery in patient with borderline resectable disease.

Gemcitabine was previously the standard adjuvant chemotherapy postresection. A new trial in Japanese patients indicates better disease control in this group with oral S1 therapy compared to gemcitabine, though it remains to be seen if this also applies in non-Asian population.

There is increasing evidence that the combination chemotherapy FOLFIRINOX (5FU, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin) achieves significantly increased survival as adjuvant therapy compared to single agent gemcitabine although it is associated with increased toxicity.

A recent trial comparing preoperative chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX to PAXG (nab-paclitaxel with platinum, capecitabine and gemcitabine) showed improved event-free survival post surgery from 10.2 to 16 months.

In patients with stage IV KRAS p.G12C–mutated pancreatic cancer who had previously been treated with chemotherapy, the KRAS G12C inhibitor sotorasib induced a response and longer progression free survival in a small stage I/II uncontrolled study.
There does remain some debate about overall benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy with a recent analysis of 459 patients failing to demonstrate improved outcome.

5FU–based chemoradiation therapy is currently recommended for patients with unresectable disease, no metastases, and good performance status.A phase 3 randomized trial demonstrates improved outcome in this group with the addition of nanoliposomal irinotecan to 5FU-based therapy, which is promising for further investigation.

In patients with a BRCA1 or 2 mutation and metastatic pancreatic cancer whose disease had not progressed after first-line chemotherapy, an RCT with 154 patients found longer progression free survival with the addition of olaparib (7.4 vs 3.8 months, p = 0.004).
Most pancreatic surgeons are willing to operate on a patient with imaging studies highly suggestive for pancreatic carcinoma, even without pathological confirmation.

Pancreatic resection is appropriate only if it is believed that all of the tumor may be removed on the basis of diagnostic studies (15%-20% of patients). Carcinoma of the pancreatic body or tail is usually too far advanced at diagnosis to consider surgery. A decision analysis found similar outcomes for neoadjuvant chemoradiation compared with resection in patients with resectable tumors (18.6 vs 17.7 months) but direct comparison studies are not available, and resection is the only potentially curative intervention.

Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) is the mainstay procedure for carcinoma of the pancreatic head. This procedure includes resection of the gastric antrum, gallbladder, common bile duct, pancreatic head, duodenum, proximal jejunum, and regional lymph nodes. This is followed by pancreaticojejunostomy, choledochojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy.

A review of 33 studies including almost 200,000 patients provides compelling evidence for survival and outcome benefit with 'centralization' of this complex surgery. A surgical caseload of 45 per annum was associated with benefit with optimal outcomes when caseload reached 70pa.
There are no data from clinical trials regarding the decision between classic Whipple procedure and pylorus preserving Whipple.
For patients requiring distal pancreatectomy, laparascopic surgery is associated with less morbidity than an open procedure, but long-term results are not known.
A review of French healthcare databases over 5 years with 2753 operations supports better outcomes with laparoscopic surgery, but this was not an RCT.

In patients with advanced disease, significant pain relief may be achieved with celiac plexus neurolysis. A Cochrane review found significant pain reduction at 4 and 8 weeks, but there was heterogeneity between studies.

A meta-analysis identified 4 studies with 818 patients comparing laparascopic with open pancreaticoduodectomy for patients with peri-ampullary tumors. The outcomes were similar other than a shorter length of stay in the laparascropic surgery group, at least in these high volume specialty centers.
Based on a systematic review of 6 studies with 358 patients, celiac plexus block may be more effective than opiates and causes fewer side effects.

For small pancreatic tumors < 2cm, usually detected as incidental findings, which may be non secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour or insulinoma, there is the option of treatment by endoscopic ultrasound guided ablation with radiofrequency ablation or ethanol ablation.
Refer for imaging studies as soon as diagnosis is suspected.
Refer to pancreatic surgeon as soon as imaging studies imply the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.

Giving somatostatin or somatostatin analogues reduces the likelihood of post-operative complications and reduces length of stay in patients undergoing pancreatic surgery. There is no evidence that their use reduces mortality, though.
If the patient is in poor medical condition or if the tumor is determined to be inoperable on initial evaluation, obstructive jaundice may be palliated by endoscopically placed metal biliary stents.

A randomized trial of patients with malignant biliary tract obstruction compared endoscopic ultrasound guided biliary drainage (EUS-BD) with ERCP. Technical and clinical success rates were similar, but EUS-BD had fewer adverse events (6% vs 20%), less post-procedure pancreatitis (0% vs 15%), less need for re-intervention (16% vs 43%) and a higher rate of stent patency (85% vs 49%).
Patients with advanced disease who develop gastric outlet obstruction may be palliated with an endoscopically placed enteral stent. Pancreatic resection is not recommended as a palliative measure.
Natural history: carcinoma of the pancreas is fatal in virtually all patients if untreated. Greater than 80% of patients present with disease that cannot be cured with surgical resection. B
A global review found that most centers perform surveillance after surgery using CT and CA 19-9. C
Even in patients who undergo surgery under optimal conditions, the median survival is 15 to 19 months, and the 5-year survival rate is about 20%. B
The strongest positive predictors for long-term survival are negative margin status (ie, R0 resection), tumor DNA content, tumor size, and absence of lymph node metastases. B
Multi-centre survival analysis confirms that both 30-day mortality post-operatively and longer term are worse in patients with tumours in the head of pancreas.
Post-operatively, monitor the patient for the onset of diabetes mellitus. C
